reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
setup: The BIS panel regression explains private credit loan origination (45 countries, 2010–2019) with four drivers: policy rate, bank-efficiency (FI) index, bank regulatory stringency and corporate leverage. The policy rate falls by **one standard deviation**, all else equal.
ask: Roughly how large is the associated change in private credit origination?

options.why: Sibling swap: ~33% per SD is the FI-index effect, the largest driver, not the policy rate.
Sibling swap: ~2–4% per SD is the regulatory-stringency effect.
Sibling swap: under 1% is the corporate-leverage effect, the weakest driver.

working.label: Policy-rate coefficient
working.display: negative ($\approx -0.03$): lower rate $\Rightarrow$ more private credit

takeaway: Per 1 SD: FI index ~33% > policy rate ~12% > stringency 2–4% > leverage <1%.

reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
setup: BIS regression, per one standard deviation: the policy rate moves private credit origination by about 12%, and bank regulatory stringency moves it by about 2–4% (use 3%). A country **cuts** its policy rate by 1 SD and at the same time **loosens** bank regulation by 1 SD.
ask: Net change in private credit origination: positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Negative
options.why: Lets the stringency leg dominate; at ~3% it only trims the ~12% rate-cut effect.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The legs are ~12% vs ~3%, a 4× gap: not close.

takeaway: Stringency coefficient is POSITIVE: looser bank rules pull borrowers back to banks, but the rate effect is ~4× bigger.

reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
setup: BIS regression, per one standard deviation: the policy rate moves private credit origination by about 12%; the FI index (how effectively banks meet loan demand) moves it by about 33%. A country's policy rate **rises** 1 SD while its FI index **falls** 1 SD.
ask: Net change in private credit origination: positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Negative
options.why: Reads a falling FI index as bad for private credit; the coefficient is negative, so weaker banks mean MORE private credit.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The legs are −12% and +33%: the FI leg is nearly 3× larger.

takeaway: Both the policy rate and the FI index carry NEGATIVE signs: weaker banks → more private credit, and FI is the biggest driver.

reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
setup: Policy rates stay low for years. Banks hold largely floating-rate assets funded by sticky, slow-repricing deposits. Private credit funds (PCFs) are floating-rate on both assets and liabilities.
ask: What happens to lending margins?

options.label: Bank margins compress; PCFs largely escape
PCF margins compress; banks escape
options.why: Role swap: the mismatched (floating vs sticky) structure is the BANK's; PCFs are matched.

options.label: Both widen
options.why: Reverses the margin effect: low rates squeeze the lender whose asset yields fall faster than its funding costs.

working.label: Bank asset yields vs deposit costs
working.display: asset yields fall faster than sticky deposit costs

working.label: Result
working.display: bank margins squeezed; PCFs (floating/floating) unaffected $\Rightarrow$ room for PCFs to lend

takeaway: Low rates squeeze banks (floating assets, sticky deposits); matched-floating PCFs slip through and fill the gap.

reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
setup: From 2010 to 2019 bank cost of equity rose sharply (market risk, stricter regulation) while BDCs swapped expensive equity for cheaper debt. Banks' traditional cost-of-capital advantage over BDCs eroded.
ask: By roughly how much did the advantage narrow?

options.label: ≈ 25 bp
options.why: Decimal slip: 2.5 percentage points read as 0.25; a quarter point would be noise.

options.label: ≈ 2,500 bp
options.why: Decimal slip the other way: 25 percentage points would be a revolution, not an erosion.

options.label: ≈ 80 bp
options.why: Scale slip (≈0.3× the truth).

takeaway: Banks' funding edge over BDCs shrank by ~250 bp (2.5 pp) over 2010–2019.

reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
setup: The ≈250 bp erosion of banks' funding advantage over BDCs (2010–2019) splits into three channels: BDCs' lower cost of equity, BDCs' increased leverage, and the cost-of-debt difference. The cost-of-debt difference stayed small, contributing ≈0 bp.
ask: Compare the cost-of-equity channel with the leverage channel: which contributed more?

options.label: Cost-of-equity channel clearly bigger
options.why: Drops the co-equal leverage channel; the reading splits the erosion roughly evenly.

options.label: Leverage channel clearly bigger
options.why: Overweights leverage; the lower BDC cost of equity pulled just as hard.

takeaway: Gap erosion: CoE and leverage ~50/50; the CoD DIFFERENCE barely moved the gap (even though cheap debt cut BDCs' own WACC).

reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
setup: BDCs replace part of their equity with debt. Their debt costs a bit more than bank debt but much less than their own equity. The extra leverage nudges BDCs' cost of equity up modestly.
ask: BDCs' overall cost of capital:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Lets the modest cost-of-equity uptick dominate; the cheaper-debt benefit more than offsets it.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: "Fully cancelled" contradicts the stated net decline in BDC cost of capital.

working.label: Substitution
working.display: expensive equity $\to$ cheaper debt: pulls WACC down

working.label: Offset
working.display: cost of equity rises modestly: pushes WACC up a little

takeaway: Debt only has to beat BDCs' OWN equity, not bank debt; the substitution lowers WACC net of the CoE uptick.

reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
setup: Policy rates rise and stay high. BDC funding costs track policy rates closely; bank deposit costs reprice slowly.
ask: Effect on the bank-vs-BDC competitive balance?

options.label: BDC cost of capital rises; the edge shifts back toward banks
BDC cost of capital falls; BDCs gain further ground
options.why: Reverses the regime shift: BDCs' cheap-debt benefit was a low-rate phenomenon.

options.label: Banks lose most, as deposit costs reprice fastest
options.why: Deposits reprice SLOWEST, which is why rising rates favor banks.

working.label: BDC debt
working.display: floats with policy rates $\Rightarrow$ funding cost up quickly

working.label: Balance
working.display: BDC cost of capital rises relative to banks'

takeaway: Higher-for-longer rates erode BDCs' cheap-debt edge; sticky deposits shelter banks.

reading: Reading 100: Advances in Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Capital Markets
setup: A stress episode hits a derivatives exchange and liquidity turns "flighty". High-frequency traders (HFTs) step back from making markets.
ask: HFT order cancellations during the episode:

options.label: Rise
options.why: The "panic = more cancelling" intuition; HFTs have withdrawn, so there are fewer standing orders to cancel.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: The reading documents a clear shift, not stability.

working.label: HFT behaviour
working.display: withdraw $\Rightarrow$ less standing activity $\Rightarrow$ fewer cancellations

working.label: Institutions (for contrast)
working.display: use MORE hidden orders to avoid moving a thin market

takeaway: Flighty liquidity: HFT cancellations DOWN, institutional hidden orders UP; both drain visible liquidity.

reading: Reading 100: Advances in Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Capital Markets
setup: Better computing hardware and algorithmic efficiency have cut the cost per unit of compute used to train AI models. At the same time, frontier models keep getting more complex.

reading: Reading 106: Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies
setup: Tokenization makes it easy for retail investors to move money out of bank deposits into tokenized financial assets.

reading: Reading 103: Global Financial Stability Report
setup: A major global geopolitical shock sends energy prices sharply higher. Consider a country that imports most of its energy.

reading: Reading 103: Global Financial Stability Report

reading: Reading 103: Global Financial Stability Report

reading: Reading 103: Global Financial Stability Report
setup: An asset is expected to GAIN value whenever geopolitical risk rises: it pays off in exactly the bad states investors fear.
ask: Its risk premium under modern asset-pricing theory:

options.label: Positive
options.why: Reverses the convention: positive premiums compensate assets that LOSE value when risk rises.

options.label: Zero, geopolitical risk is not priced

takeaway: Hedges carry negative premiums; assets that crater in bad states carry positive ones.
